paragraphs: When news of the Qin army’s rout reached Jiankang, a boat laden with newly harvested rice happened to lose its rudder on the Qinhuai River. The sailors shouted for help along the bank; more than a dozen people put out poles, struggling for a long while before they could haul the boat into the shallows. The owner was cursing himself hoarse when a cheer rose by the city gate on the north bank: “Victory on the Huai!”
He stood dazed a moment, let go of his rope, and laughed too. His boatful of rice drifted sideways again and nearly struck another man’s pleasure barge.
Xie An was listening to an elderly clerk when the report came.

The clerk had been ordered to reconcile the grain levies for the Beifu Army, and one entry in his registers simply would not balance. Xie An did not hurry him; he only asked for fresh tea. In the distance the drums of the palace city grew faster. At last a messenger carried in the victory dispatch: Xie Xuan had cut the Qin pontoon bridges, and Peng Chao was withdrawing north. Xie An turned to the next page, paused under the figures for Qin casualties, and asked, “And ours?”
“We have suffered losses as well,” the messenger replied, “but the count is not complete.”
“If it is not complete, don’t write in a conveniently small number just to please us.”

He laid the dispatch aside and invited the old clerk to continue explaining how two hundred shi of rice had disappeared between two granaries. The messenger stood under the veranda clutching his helmet, listening in puzzlement as the city drums swelled again and again. Those who had served Xie An for years were accustomed to it: Lord Xie seldom displayed joy or grief at the moment when others expected him to.
The beginning of this victory had been the defeat at Xiangyang the year before.

Summer still lay heavy upon the south when the dispatch boat came downriver through the night. The report that reached the palace city made painful reading: Li Bohu had secretly opened the gates; Zhu Xu had fought hard and been captured; Jin forces had withdrawn south of the Han River. Several elder ministers declared that the Qin must have massacred Xiangyang and urged that the people of Jiangling be moved at once into the hills and marshes, denying the enemy provisions. But travelers from Jingzhou brought statements from fugitives who said that Qin officers had executed soldiers for plunder. Blood had been shed in the city, but the army had not been turned loose to pillage it. The two sides quarreled in court so fiercely that they nearly accused one another of being Qin agents.
Sima Yao grew impatient. “Which account are we supposed to believe?” he asked Xie An.
“Keep both sets of witnesses here,” Xie An replied.
“What do you mean?”
“Those who escaped know what they themselves saw, not necessarily what happened in the whole city. Those who never went there have even less right to swear on behalf of everyone in it.”

He put both statements under his papers, noting the travelers' names, their routes, and the wards where they had stayed in Xiangyang, and ordered Jiangling to inquire further. If the Qin army truly restrained its men by military discipline, Xiangyang would not be recovered merely by holding a single wall. If its reputation for mercy was only a veil, its surveys of land, deeds, and grain collection would expose that soon enough.
While the court competed to assign blame for the lost city, Xie An was investigating timber.

In recent years shipbuilding at Jiankang had consumed much of the large timber along the river. Craftsmen floated beams down from upstream, and prices rose rapidly. Xie An summoned the official in charge of boats and asked how many vessels capable of navigating shallow water could be used if three thousand more boatmen were called up. The official said the large ships were enough to cover the face of the river. Xie An took him down to a landing and pointed at several little craft on the mudflats, each of which two men could drag. “And these?”
“Fishing boats belonging to commoners. They cannot serve as warships.”

Xie An had a boatman push one into the water, then made the official watch it swing around beneath the towering side of a larger ship. One shove of the pole, half a turn of the bow, and it vanished into the reeds. The watchers on shore could not even see the backs of its two occupants.
“Have Xie Xuan come see for himself,” Xie An said.

When Xie Xuan reached Jiankang, there was still mud from Guangling on the hem of his clothes. He examined charts sent in from the provinces. What interested him most was not the blue lines marking rivers, but the blank spaces. On one map a river had been drawn perfectly straight. He sent for the draughtsman, who explained that the county had so many small channels they could hardly all be recorded. Xie Xuan rolled up the chart and went to ask the boatmen. A woman who made her living gathering reeds said there was a narrow branch channel in front of her home. When the waters rose in summer, a boat could pass behind two scholar trees and reach the southern embankment directly. The official map had not been revised for thirty years. The trees had grown in the meantime.

Xie Xuan offered to pay her to guide a boat through. An attendant protested that such an errand was beneath a general’s dignity. “If you can drag the entire army out of the mud,” Xie Xuan said, “I’ll pay you too.”

What Xie An had to settle in Jiankang was whether this army could survive at all. The Beifu recruits included northern refugees and famine fugitives whose household registrations had been lost. The moment anyone in court proposed granting them farmland, others worried that the burden on established southern households would grow. With no clan genealogies to support their claims, the refugees were asked by land officials where their ancestors were buried and who their former neighbors had been. Some could not answer and waited at the office doors day after day.

A woman with two children came to Xie An’s residence to complain. Her husband had been enlisted, but the military administration would not issue her a soldier’s household ration: the old register still listed him in a county north of the Huai, and his transferred records had not reached Guangling. She spoke with a northern accent that two young clerks at the gate scarcely understood. Xie An happened to be leaving. He ordered three days' grain issued to her first, and had the old register sent to the officer responsible for verifying households. He would not allow the gatekeepers to send her away with the words “no registration.” The woman thanked him repeatedly, but there was no gladness in her face. She did not know where she could go after those three days.
“If Beifu is to have soldiers, it must first have families for those soldiers,” Xie An told Xie Xuan later. “What the court has given you are living people, not a register already filled out.”

Gradually the Beifu camps changed. Not every new northern recruit could handle water. A man who had spent his life on horseback might nearly vomit when he first stood on a boat’s planks. A fisherman who could row expertly might scarcely hold a sword and lose all composure at the beat of a war drum. Xie Xuan assigned both kinds of men to the same squads and made their first lesson the rescue of someone overboard. During one water drill a soldier tangled in the rope struggled and choked. An officer was ready to punish him, but Xie Xuan held out his hand, rolled up his trousers, stepped into the water himself, and asked the man who had tied the rope, “Did you ever test whether this knot tightens when it gets wet?”
The man’s face turned white. That day the entire camp changed its way of fastening boat ropes.

At first there were few glorious victories for the Beifu Army. More often the men crawled through reeds beside gray water, tended campfires that would not light because the wood was damp, and learned how to keep their straw sandals on their feet in the mud. Small scouting parties tested the Qin supply routes and returned as soon as they learned what they needed. They did not rush a town wall or chase a fleeing enemy. A young officer finally asked whether the court had given them troops merely to hide inside boats. Xie Xuan took him to see a warhorse trapped in a mire. Several soldiers supported it beneath the belly, but all four hooves remained sunk fast.
“Northern horsemen come here wanting to fight the battles they know,” Xie Xuan said. “If you ride out, you give them just such a battle. If you don’t, they must come in after you.”

Some called Xie Xuan’s method deceitful and unworthy of a great army fighting in the open. He took no offense. He only ordered each camp to mark the daily rise and fall of the river on wooden boards. Anyone who got the marks wrong three days in a row was sent to help fishermen dry their nets. Within months some soldiers could judge the depth of water by the color of the reed leaves, more surely than they remembered the bridges listed in the local gazetteers.

When Peng Chao’s vanguard was trapped at the river stockade, Xie Xuan was not on the heights. He went himself along a shallow branch channel to inspect the returning wounded. Jin soldiers carried back three men on a boat plank. A Qin crossbow bolt had gone through one man’s leg bone, and he had bitten his wooden gag to splinters from the pain. Xie Xuan asked why they had gone so near the enemy camp. The squad leader admitted that, hoping for credit, he had pursued a band of fugitives and nearly let a Qin crossbow ambush cut off his retreat. Xie Xuan ordered the offense recorded under military law, then had their bleeding stopped. The squad leader tried to kneel. Xie Xuan told him to steady the stretcher instead.
“The men are alive. Get them back first. Kneeling won’t make your offense any lighter.”

Later, when the Qin floating bridges broke and twenty thousand vanguard troops were trapped, Xie Xuan still did not attack at once. His generals begged to strike in the confusion, certain they could cut down ten thousand men. Instead he kept the boatmen on the river and forbade the infantry on the heights from descending without orders, above all to chase scattered soldiers away from the crossing. Whenever someone pressed for permission, Xie Xuan asked how many days of grain they could carry. Only on the third morning, while the mist still hung low, did he send the detachments in boats to intercept the breakout. Friend and enemy banners became confused in the fog, and many Jin soldiers fell into the river. Xie Xuan separated a portion of the flotilla to rescue them and forbade every boat from joining the pursuit. After the sun had passed its height, Qin retreat drums sounded from the north bank.

Victory dispatches traveled all the way to Jiankang. Xie Xuan himself did not return with the triumphant riders. He stayed in Guangling to count the camp boats. When his generals asked to choose a few fine horses from the captured Qin baggage as rewards, he agreed, but ordered the captive medical artisans sent to the wounded camp first. While inspecting the spoils, an official found a book labeled *Newly Organized Qin Infantry*. Inside were the names of Di, Xianbei, Qiang, and Han men serving in the same squads. Someone laughed that they ate from one pot and, when they died, made no distinction among themselves either. Xie Xuan told him to wrap up the register and send it to Jiankang with the dispatch.
In autumn, Xie Xuan was summoned back to the capital.

Wuyi Lane was ablaze with lanterns, and guests offering congratulations crowded the street outside the Xie residence. Pleading ill health, Xie An received visitors only in the eastern gallery. Xie Xuan passed through two courtyards and found his uncle playing a board game with a younger kinsman. A white stone had advanced deep among the black stones, several of which were poised to surround it. Xie Xuan bowed. Xie An motioned him to sit, and finished the game before speaking.
“How are the boats?” Xie An asked.
“They can manage the flood, but they still fear the autumn wind.”
“And the Beifu soldiers?”
“They no longer fear the river. But at the sight of heavy Qin crossbows, some still drop flat and cannot bring themselves to rise.”
“What will you do?”
“Keep drilling through the winter.”

Xie An nodded and ordered a bowl of hot broth brought in. When uncle and nephew came to the floating bridge on the Huai, Xie Xuan casually took a bowl of game stones from beside the board and arranged them to show the embankment, riverbank, and grain camp. Several Qin units, he said, had withdrawn in good order, and some mixed squads had shielded their comrades all the way back. If the Qin repaired several roads ahead of time, gathered enough boats, and returned under a different commander, the river might not fight this battle for Jin a second time.
Hearing this, Xie An seemed to relax.
“Good. You have not mistaken the river for a divine weapon of your own.”

They were silent a while. From outside the hall came clapping and cheers: the banquet in the front courtyard was not over. Xie Xuan asked, “They are celebrating so loudly tonight. If we must fight again next year, how much grain will the court grant us?”
“Go and ask them,” Xie An said.
“I have. Some want the army disbanded; others are afraid I command too many men.”
“Then write down clearly how many soldiers you must keep, how many boats you must replace, how many granaries you must build.”
“And if they still refuse?”
“Invite them to live in Guangling for a month and taste the rain on the river.”

Xie Xuan laughed, but the smile soon faded. He picked up the captured Qin register and said that after the battle he had seen Qin soldiers carrying one another across the water. Though they could not speak one another’s languages, they recognized the waist tallies of men from their own camps. The court dismissed the Qin army as a makeshift gathering of barbarian horsemen, unaware that its soldiers now fought better than before and were more willing to hold to their orders until death.

Xie An turned a few pages and stopped at one soldier’s birthplace. The man had originally lived on Jin soil, then followed his father north; now he had died in the Qin ranks. Xie An asked whether his family remained in the south. Xie Xuan shook his head. The record said only that he had once had a wife and children, with no indication where their household had been transferred.
“Keep this for him,” Xie An said, closing the register. “If someone comes looking after the war, there must be somewhere they can ask.”

Soon enough, someone at court impeached the Xie clan for monopolizing military authority, arguing that if the refugee soldiers of Beifu remained under Xie Xuan’s command indefinitely, the state might be endangered. At the hearing the accuser spoke with great heat. Xie An neither reached for a sword nor flared into anger. He simply presented Sima Yao with two registers sent by Xie Xuan: one listed the old and new boats of the Beifu flotilla, the other dated Qin movements on and off the Huai banks.
“Your Majesty,” Xie An said, “if you choose a worthier commander, I will gladly surrender this command. I ask only that these boats first be entrusted to someone who understands water.”
“But how can the great clans feel secure while the Xie command so much military strength?” another official asked.

“If you fear Xie Xuan, send grain inspectors to audit his stores and censors to inspect his troops. But if you break up trained river soldiers and give them to men who know nothing of the river, you will not be investigating the Xie clan. You will be doing Fu Jian’s work for him.”

Several ministers withdrew in anger. Sima Yao ultimately permitted Beifu to continue its training, strengthened the auditing of military rolls and pay, and required the Jiang-Huai commanderies to report each season on damaged boats and repairs to the levees. Xie Xuan accepted the edict and returned to Guangling as before, without one more word in defense of his commander’s seal.

Nor did the defeat of the Qin bring comfort to everyone. Military families in Jiangling who had lost loved ones wrote demanding to know why Xiangyang remained in Qin hands when the south had won on the Huai. Xie An forwarded their letters to the Jingzhou command, asking for a reply that counted how many refugees outside the walls still had nowhere to go. Some advisers proposed issuing a fierce proclamation denouncing Qin cruelty to reassure the people. Xie An asked for the statements of fugitives from Xiangyang, read several pages, and said only, “They are telling us what happened to their own families. Do not invent another calamity in their name that none of them saw.”

The Jin army had won a river battle, yet in the mansions of the great clans at Jiankang there were still fine horses bought from Qin territory, and people who called northern refugees baseborn and would not let them cross their thresholds. Xie An knew it. If the court would not change, there might not be so many willing to defend Jiankang the next time an invader came.

From then on, officials examining wagon wheels, timber, and iron hooks appeared along the trade route from Jiankang to Guangling. Spies no longer merely counted northern banners. They asked how sharply carriage prices had risen in Luoyang, which granary doors were sealed in Guanzhong, and why packhorses from Hedong were so slow to leave their stalls. Most of the reports seemed trivial; even the couriers did not know what purpose they served. Xie An had them posted by date on the wall. Whenever one item matched something recorded months earlier, he asked a secretary to draw a thin line of ink beside it.

One early-winter day Xie An climbed the walls of Stone City and saw the north wind driving several white sails that had not yet been furled on the Yangtze. Xie Xuan followed him and asked whether the Qin would come again.
“They will.”
“When?”
“That depends on Chang’an.”
“What if Fu Jian truly brings the armies of his entire realm?”

Xie An did not answer immediately. He watched the landing below. Laborers carrying salt were dragging a battered boat up the beach. Seven or eight men shouted in rhythm and heaved with all their strength, but the ebb tide had left it stuck in the mud. Someone suggested calling another ten men. The master craftsman took up a hoe instead and dug a narrow channel beneath the hull. Water trickled along it, and the boat rose an inch.
Only then did Xie An speak. “First find the right way through. However great the boat, shouting louder will not haul it over a shallow bank.”

Xie Xuan followed his gaze. The Yangtze stretched vast before them. Smoke and dust had not yet cleared from the southern shore, and no enemy banner could be seen to the north. At the landing the workmen had pushed their boat into the water. They cheered once, then each returned to his labor.

Back at the residence, Xie An set a white stone on the unfinished board, but did not use the stone deep in the black formation to launch an attack. He placed a supporting stone behind it. The younger kinsman studied the board and could not help asking whether this was not too slow.
Xie An smiled. “That stone is not alive yet. Let it live first. Then we can think about whose territory to take.”
